title: Before sleep
hook: a traditional Jewish bedtime prayer begins by forgiving anyone who hurt you that day

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mara, and Naomi's story told twice. Your line was a new telling. Today, a practice for the end of every day, before the stories pile up.

What does the mind do in the last minutes before sleep? Lights off, phone down, and the day starts replaying. The comment in the meeting. The text that was a little too short. The friend who didn't ask how it went. Small things, mostly. But small things left overnight have a way of being bigger by morning, and bigger still by the end of the week. A Jewish tradition has an answer built into bedtime itself. Before the Shema is said at night, a prayer comes first, and it opens with forgiveness.
screen: `LIGHTS OFF. THE DAY REPLAYS.` → `SMALL THINGS GROW OVERNIGHT.` → `A PRAYER AT THE BEDSIDE.`

segments.voice: First, where it sits. The bedtime Shema is a set of prayers said at night, at home, often in bed. In the traditional prayer book, before the Shema itself, there's a short passage addressed to the Master of the world. Second, what it says. In paraphrase: I hereby forgive anyone who angered me or wronged me, whether against my body, my property or my honor, by accident or on purpose, in word or in deed. It doesn't ask who deserves it, and it isn't limited to today. It covers the whole list in one sweep. Third, the line that surprises people. The prayer goes further: it asks that no one be punished on my account. Not just I let it go, but I don't want them to suffer because of what they did to me. That's a big request to make about someone who was rude to you at lunch, and it's said at night, while the day's grudges are still fresh. Fourth, a neighbor. Christians read a line from the letter to the Ephesians that points at the same hour: "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath." Two traditions, each in its own words, both asking that the day's anger be set down at the edge of night. Clear the small debts daily, the way you'd wash the dishes before bed, so you don't wake up to a sink full of them.
screen: `A PRAYER BEFORE THE SHEMA.` · `BODY, PROPERTY, HONOR.` · `LET NO ONE BE PUNISHED FOR ME.` · `NOT THE SUN ON YOUR WRATH.` · then, large: `I FORGIVE TODAY.`

segments.voice: Whatever the hour, sit as if it were the end of the day, and flip back through today, or yesterday if it's morning, like photos. At each small sting, a word, a look, a silence, don't argue the case; just say silently, I forgive today, and move to the next. If something is too big for tonight, set it aside, and if you pray, you can use a bedtime prayer from your own tradition.
Before sleep. The last minutes of the day, when a Jewish bedtime prayer forgives the day's wrongs before the Shema is said. Today's word.
Your line: I forgive today. Small debts, cleared before they pile up. Day nine hundred ninety-two, done.

chat.says: Why say a forgiveness prayer at bedtime? Most days nobody did anything that bad.
options: That's the point: small stings cleared each night don't grow by morning.
It's only for big wrongs; small stings are too minor to bother forgiving.
It's really for asking God to punish whoever wronged you that day.

notes: The forgiveness passage before the bedtime Shema (Ribbono shel olam, hareini mochel…) is paraphrased; confirm the paraphrase (body, property, honor; accident or on purpose; word or deed; no one punished on my account) against a standard siddur.
Hebrew הֲרֵינִי מוֹחֵל: confirm pointing; the passage begins Ribbono shel olam, and these words follow.
'often in bed' and 'said at night, at home': confirm wording.
Ephesians 4:26 is introduced as a neighbor sharing the theme, not a comparison.
Editor pass: Ephesians 4:26 speaks of anger, not forgiveness, so the comparison line now says both set the day's anger down before night.

Audit pass: the prayer forgives any wrong, not only that day's (it adds 'whether in this incarnation or another'), so howItsDone and the teach no longer limit it to the day. Many siddurim word it as forgiving 'every person of Israel' (kol bar Yisrael), others 'every person'; the paraphrase says 'anyone', so a Keeper should confirm. 'Paul's letter to the Ephesians' changed to 'the letter to the Ephesians', since its authorship is debated. Review updated to day 991's new Ruth story.
